title: Hallucination Inc.: I made a satirical strategy game with Claude Code agents. Here's what worked and what didn't
author: tweeto
selftext:
Play: [https://hallucinc.com](https://hallucinc.com) (free, browser, phone or desktop, no sign-up)

The game: you run an AI lab from 2021 to 2026. Each quarter one memo lands on your desk, you sign one of two or three answers with the price printed on each, place one bet, and the news reports what you did. 24 quarters, about 12 minutes. Going public is the consolation prize.

How I made it: I wrote the design document and made every call, and Claude Code wrote the code, the cards and the jokes, with several agents working in parallel, each in its own folder.

The thing that made it work wasn't the model, it was the paperwork. There's one file every agent reads first with the rules of the project, and a management folder with the current status, the open questions and every decision with its date. Without that, each new session forgot why things were the way they were and undid them.

The second thing was making the game checkable. The simulation is pure TypeScript with a seeded random generator, so the same seed and the same choices always give the same run, and saved replays catch any change to the balance nobody meant to make. Bots play a lot of runs after every content change, and a linter checks every card. Nothing reaches players without passing types, tests, a size budget and a browser test suite, then a staging copy, and production only when I say so.

What didn't work: agents report "done" on things nobody actually verified, so every report gets checked before it's committed. And the hardest part wasn't the code at all, it was making the first minute clear to a new player. My stats say most visitors still leave on the first card, so that's what I'm on now.

Happy to answer questions about the setup, and I'd love to hear where your first run stopped making sense.
